metadata.title: Claude, BigQuery API.
metadata.purpose: Answer whether a Claude BigQuery query is one instant call or a tracked job, using the BigQuery API skill's own documented facts as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that every job turns on two habits — carrying location on every follow-up call, and checking for an error before trusting DONE.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (top-10-names-California job, traced through billing project + location, then checked correctly vs. DONE-but-failed)

beats.narration_text: People walk in thinking a BigQuery query is one API call, rows back. Wrong branch. Every query becomes a tracked job — checked and paged until it's ready. So what does that job actually look like?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude must just make one API call and hand back my rows. Is that it?', hesitates on 'call', corrects to 'job', lands the real question

beats.narration_text: Ask Claude for the top ten names in a public dataset and sometimes rows come straight back — that's synchronous mode, one request that blocks the connection until it's done. It optimizes for the fast case, and it fails the moment your query isn't fast. So the API switches contract: a slower query submits instead, a job with its own ID, checked and paged until it's ready. Two modes, one endpoint — the design pushes the boundary between fast-enough and not onto the client to notice.

shot.new_visual_element: Sync mode shown as one blocking call; when the window runs out, a job card with its own ID appears in its place

production_viz.label: One call, or a tracked job
production_viz.mechanic: A single request card blocks, spins briefly, and returns rows — labelled SYNCHRONOUS. A second, slower request hits a timeout mark and instead spawns a job card with an ID stamped on it, labelled ASYNCHRONOUS, checked and paged over time.

beats.narration_text: That job runs inside a billing project — the project charged for bytes scanned isn't necessarily where the data lives — and it's pinned to the location it ran in. Two anchors, deliberately separate: who pays, and what region the job belongs to. Ask for the top ten names in California from the public names dataset, and every later check on that job has to carry that same location back, or it 404s. Region is a hard boundary here, not a hint — the design chose strict locality over convenience, and pushed the carrying onto you.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — the 'top 10 names, California' job traced: billing project pays, location pins the job, every follow-up call carries that same location

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — billing project pays, location pins it
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A job card labelled 'top 10 names · California' sits between two tags: BILLING PROJECT (pays) pointing at the job, and a separate DATA tag off to the side (lives elsewhere). A LOCATION stamp locks onto the job. Every later request arrow drawn from the job back out carries that same location stamp with it. THIS EXACT JOB RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Check that same job with the location attached and it comes back clean. But here's the trap: reaching DONE means the job finished, not that it succeeded. The response carries an errorResult field, and that gets read before the rows are trusted — otherwise a failed job looks identical to a successful one. Symmetric mistake on the other side: a job still marked RUNNING isn't proof it's stuck — that's what the polling is for. And one honest wart in the API: the field name for "more pages" isn't the same everywhere. List endpoints use nextPageToken; a query's own results use pageToken. Read the wrong one and it comes back empty, silently, after page one. This works if you check both signals every time; it fails the moment you trust a status without reading the payload.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same job checked correctly and cleared, then DONE-but-failed flagged, then the pagination field-name split broken out as the one exception

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — clean, then DONE-but-failed, then the one exception
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 JOB RETURNS, identical, location stamp attached, checked and cleared — labelled DONE, no error. Beside it, the same job shape marked DONE but with an errorResult flag lit terracotta — 'looks finished' even though it isn't. A small card breaks off to the side: 'nextPageToken (lists) vs pageToken (query results)' — the one naming split that doesn't match the rest.

beats.narration_text: Every BigQuery job Claude runs turns on two habits — carry the same location on every follow-up call, and check for an error before trusting a job marked done — get those right and both query modes take care of themselves.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to run a BigQuery query end-to-end against the public dataset bigquery-public-data.usa_names.usa_1910_current and return the top five names for Texas — walk me through carrying the same location on every follow-up call to that job, reading errorResult before trusting a status of DONE, and handling the pagination field-name split between nextPageToken for list endpoints and pageToken for query results. Give me a small Python snippet I could actually run, with comments marking where each of those three checks lives. Go deeper: ask the same model what breaks first if the billing project you're paying from doesn't have the BigQuery Jobs API enabled — where does that failure surface, and does it look like an auth error, a 404, or something else? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to run a BigQuery query end-to-end and understand exactly what a naive client gets wrong. Run a query against the public dataset bigquery-public-data.usa_names.usa_1910_current and return the top five names for Texas. Walk me through three things a robust client has to handle: (1) carrying the same location on every follow-up call to that job, (2) reading the errorResult field before trusting a status of DONE, and (3) using the correct pagination field — nextPageToken for list endpoints, pageToken for query results — so it doesn't silently return an empty page after page one. Give me a small Python snippet I could actually run, with comments marking where each of those three checks lives.
